title: Microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of V-containing medium-Mn steel manufactured via cold rolling and intercritical annealing
abstract: V was added into a cold-rolled medium-Mn steel for optimizing comprehensive mechanical properties by the V-carbide precipitation. After annealing, the V-carbide particles in austenite grains easily coarsen than that in ferrite. The contributed yield strength increment of V-carbide precipitation strengthening in ferrite is in a range of 200–250 MPa. With increasing annealing temperature, the morphology of ferrite and austenite gradually transforms from lamellar to equiaxed. The sample after intercritical annealing at 650 °C shows 1450 MPa ultimate tensile strength, 1210 MPa yield strength, and 18% tensile elongation. In addition, samples with lamellar and equiaxed structures display larger Lüders plateaus than samples with a single equiaxed/lamellar structure. Partial martensitic transformation and continuous interactions between dislocation and twin are responsible for the Lüders plateau propagation. Therein, the number fraction of coarse austenite grains should be responsible for the propagation of Lüders plateau.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High strength and ductility materials have always been the goal of the industry. However, the increase of strength will inevitably result in the sacrifice of plasticity. Medium-Mn steel is considered the new generation of high-strength steel due to its excellent mechanical properties and good economy [ 1 , 2 ]. Medium-Mn steels, whose Mn content is in the range of 5%–10%, can expand the austenite phase region in the equilibrium phase diagram, so it has a wide annealing temperature range [ 3 ]. Ordinarily, austenite can contribute to high work hardening behavior and delay necking through martensitic transformation, which is considered the critical factor for determining the mechanical properties [ 4 , 5 ]. Intercritical annealing is an effective way to improve the comprehensive mechanical properties of medium-Mn steels by adjusting austenite stability and forming nano-scale precipitates [ 6 , 7 ]. The structure of cold-rolled medium-Mn steel after intercritical annealing is composed of ferrite and austenite (two-phase) grains. Both the two-phase structure and the generations of transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) effects in austenite during tensile deformation continuously promote work hardening and improve the mechanical properties of medium-Mn steels [ 6 , 8 , 9 ]. Therefore, how to reasonably tailor the volume fraction and stability of austenite is critical. However, too high austenite stability may slow down the transformation kinetics of austenite to martensite and not provide enough work hardening [ 10 ]. Similarly, excessive austenite content may soften the matrix and not provide continuous work hardening. Moreover, austenite stability is closely related to its morphology. Kim et al. [ 11 ] reported a Fe-2.11Mn-0.81Al-0.2C-1.49Si-0.035Ti-0.045Nb-0.22V (wt.%) medium-Mn steel with 30% total elongation (TE) and 1.2 GPa ultimate tensile strength (UTS). They found equiaxed structures exhibit discontinuous yielding while lamellar structures exhibit continuous yielding [ 11 ]. Li et al. [ 8 ] reported a high UTS × TE value of 70 GPa·% for Fe-6Mn-2Al-0.4C (wt.%) medium-Mn steel. Such outstanding properties were attributed to the bimodal-size austenite. The ductility of above medium-Mn steels is greatly enhanced; however, the strength is limited.

Precipitation strengthening can effectively contribute to the strength of medium-Mn steel. Hu et al. [ 9 ] reported that the contributed yield strength (YS) increments of nano-size VC precipitation strengthening in both ferrite and austenite of a Fe-10Mn-2Al-0.47C-0.7V (wt.%) steel are higher than 300 MPa. Especially, ultrafine V-carbide precipitates (<20 nm) in intra-granular ferrite could greatly accelerate the enhancement of strength [ 9 ]. Zhang et al. [ 12 ] reported that intercritical annealing resulted in a dense distribution of high-density nano NiAl precipitates at the boundaries of ferrite and austenite, particularly at the ferrite side, improving the strength of a Fe-0.2C-7Mn-3Al-3Ni (wt.%) medium-Mn steel. Li et al. [ 13 ] investigated the effect of hierarchical nano-size precipitates (spherical NiAl/Cu co-particles and lenticular Cu/Ni particles) on the tempered Fe-0.01C-7Mn-2.5Ni-1.5Al-1.5Cu (wt.%) steel. The contributed YS increment of these nano-size precipitates was in the range of 500–700 MPa [ 13 ]. In addition, the pre-existing austenite played a role in the precipitate evolution during isothermal holding [ 14 ]. The nano-size precipitates act as an obstacle to grain growth during recrystallization [ 15 ]. In other words, there is a complex relationship between nano-size precipitates and austenite grains. Unfortunately, such a complicated relationship has not been clearly revealed so far. In conclusion, the purpose of exploring the above-mentioned relationship is to develop a super-high strength and ductility medium-Mn steel. Therefore, if we can employ precipitation strengthening to improve the strength and tailor austenite stability to optimize the ductility using intercritical annealing, a medium-Mn steel with ideal mechanical properties will be manufactured.

In this paper, the Fe-10.2Mn-2Al-0.4C-0.6V (wt.%) medium-Mn steel after intercritical annealing is investigated. The relationship between microstructure evolution containing V-carbide particles and mechanical properties has been expounded.

sections.heading: Experiment
paragraphs: The material was prepared to be melted and cast in a vacuum furnace in Taiyuan Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. The variation of austenite volume fraction with temperature is simulated by JMatPro software. The temperature of the 50% austenite phase content is 615 °C, and the A 3  value is 800 °C. In addition, the cementite and V-carbide dissolve absolutely at 620 and 1060 °C, respectively. These simulated temperatures have an important guiding role in the subsequent heat-treatment process.

The process and microstructure evolution diagrams of rolling and intercritical annealing is shown in  Fig. 1 
                      . The 30 mm thickness billet was held at 1200 °C for 2 h. The microstructure is composed of austenite, as shown in  Fig. 1 a, then hot-rolling to 3 mm thickness between 1050 and 800 °C before air-cooling to room temperature (RT). The microstructure is composed of austenite and ferrite, as shown in  Fig. 1 b. The hot-rolled plate was cold-rolled to 1.6 mm thickness. Partial ferrite grains were crushed to refine grains and martensite formed by strain-induced, as shown in  Fig. 1 c. After that, the cold-rolled samples were heated to 600, 650, 700 and 750 °C for 10 min before air-cooling to RT, separately. The ultrafine ferrite reversely transformed into austenite during annealing process, as shown in  Fig. 1 d, then the austenite was retained after cooling, as shown in  Fig. 1 e. The corresponding samples were abbreviated as I600, I650, I700, and I750, respectively.

Samples of 6 mm width and 25 mm length were used for tensile testing on a WDW-200 tensile testing machine (Mei Te Si Co. Ltd., Jinan, China) along the rolling direction at a speed of 0.5 mm/min. Microstructure of the annealed samples was characterized by X-ray Diffraction (XRD) using Cu Kα radiation on a Rigaku Smart Lab SE diffractometer at 40 kV, 30 mA. The XRD data, including the peaks, angle, full-width at half maximum (FWHM), and integral strength of the diffraction peaks were analyzed using the Jade 6.0 software. The observation of the samples was examined with a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM; Tescan Mira 3, Tescan, Brno, Czech Republic) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system (Oxford). EBSD and SEM specimens were mechanically polished and etched in a solution of 4% HNO 3  and 96% C 2 H 5 OH. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM; JEM 2100F, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) samples were prepared by electro-polishing and observed at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. TEM specimens were mechanically polished and etched in the above-mixed solution at −25 °C.

sections.heading: SEM microstructure
paragraphs:
The annealed microstructures are composed of body centered cubic (BCC) and face centered cubic (FCC) phases, as shown in  Fig. 2 
                            . With the increase of annealing temperature, the lamellar morphology gradually transforms into equiaxed morphology. Almost only lamellar austenite and ferrite grains are observed in sample I600 ( Fig. 2 a). However, sample I650 is composed of austenite and ferrite with lamellar and equiaxed morphologies ( Fig. 2 b). Some coarse (>1 μm) and fine (<1 μm) austenite grains are observed in sample I650 ( Fig. 2 b). The former should be the previous austenite grains that were retained, while the latter is formed from the reverse transformation of previous martensite/ferrite grains or the recrystallization of coarse austenite grains. A few lamellar austenite/ferrite grains and more equiaxed austenite/ferrite grains are observed in sample I700 ( Fig. 2 c). When the temperature increases to 750 °C, the lamellar grains almost completely disappear and are replaced by the equiaxed austenite and ferrite grains ( Fig. 2 d).

sections.heading: TEM microstructure
paragraphs:
TEM images of the hot-rolled and cold-rolled samples are shown in  Fig. S1 . Few or even no V-carbide particles were observed in the hot-rolled sample ( Fig. S1(a) ). In contrast, more ultrafine nano-size V-carbide particles are observed in the cold-rolled sample, as shown in  Fig. S1(b)  (the marked areas with white ellipses).  Fig. 3 
                             depicts that the nano V-carbide particles densely precipitate in austenite and ferrite grains after intercritical annealing. They may precipitate along dislocations and grain boundaries during cold rolling through strain-induced precipitation [ 16 ] or even during annealing [ 17 ]. Ferrite grain with the size of 100–500 nm is embedded within or between coarse austenite grains of sample I650 ( Fig. 3 a). In contrast, some coarse V-carbide particles (>30 nm) are observed in austenite grains, which may be the fact that the abundant C element in austenite is more conducive to V-carbide nucleation and growth during cold rolling or intercritical annealing. Interestingly, ultrafine nano V-carbide particles, having the size of 10–20 nm, are observed in fine ferrite grains. The enlarged image of the marked area with a red rectangle in  Fig. 3 a is shown in  Fig. 3 b, suggesting that the ultrafine V-carbide particles precipitate later in fine ferrite grains due to the high supersaturation of C and V elements. In addition, dislocation tangles are observed around the fine ferrite and austenite grains ( Fig. 3 b). This result may be due to the suppressive influence of fine ferrite and austenite grains on dislocations. When the temperature increases to 700 °C, dislocations are observed along austenite and ferrite grain boundaries ( Fig. 3 c), and the enlarged image of the marked area in  Fig. 3 c reveals that nano V-carbide precipitates are distributed in coarse austenite grains surrounded by dense dislocation forests ( Fig. 3 d). Further increasing temperature to 750 °C, more nano V-carbide particles precipitate and coarsen in austenite grains, and the distribution of V-carbide particles is more uneven ( Fig. 3 e). In addition, dislocation cells are observed along the grain boundaries ( Fig. 3 e). The enlarged image in  Fig. 3 e shows that coarse V-carbide particles (>30 nm) are embedded in the polygonal austenite grains surrounded by ferrite grains ( Fig. 3 f).

sections.heading: EBSD microstructure
paragraphs: EBSD microstructure of cold-rolled sample is given in  Fig. S2 . The ultrafine ferrite grains with equiaxed morphology are located within coarse ferrite grains ( Fig. S2(a) ).  Fig. S2(b)  shows the orientation image of BCC phase. The orientations of ultrafine ferrite grains are extremely different from that of nearby coarse ferrite grains. Such a result can be used to confirm the reliability of  Fig. 1 c.

EBSD phase (austenite and ferrite) maps of samples I650, I700, and I750 are shown in  Fig. 4 
                            a–c. The measured average grain sizes of samples I650, I700, and I750 are 0.23 ± 0.05, 0.34 ± 0.07, and 0.48 ± 0.11 μm, respectively. EBSD kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps of samples I650, I700, and I750 are shown in  Fig. 4 d–f. KAM maps are considered a measure of strain-induced local orientation gradients, and the maximum misorientation angle is 5° [ 18 ]. Austenite grains in samples show high KAM values, while ferrite grains show low KAM values. High KAM valued regions containing elongated grains and low KAM valued regions containing equiaxed grains can be defined as non-recrystallized and recrystallized regions, respectively [ 19 ]. Partial recrystallization of ferrite occurs in sample I650. With the increasing annealing temperature, most of the ferrite grains are recrystallized in samples I700 and I750. Especially in sample I750, a high volume fraction of recrystallized ferrite grains leads to a low KAM value and an increased number of grains.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 6 
                          shows the engineering strain–stress curves of samples. The YS and UTS decrease obviously with the increasing annealing temperature, while the TE increases from 1.6% in sample I600 to 18% in sample I650, and then decreases to 8.6% in sample I750. Except for sample I600, both the Lüders plateau and Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) band are observed in other samples. In contrast, the sample with lamellar and equiaxed structures shows the best combination of strength and ductility; the sample with lamellar structure shows higher strength and lower ductility than the sample with equiaxed structure, indicating that the mechanical properties strongly depend on the microstructure morphology caused by annealing temperature [ 1 , 5 , 9 , 11 ].

Obviously, the dislocation strengthening decreases with the increasing annealing temperature; this result is consistent with  Fig. 3 . sections.heading: Other strengthening
paragraphs:
Fig. 9 
                             shows the contributed YS increments of  σ 
                            P ,  σ 
                            D,  and other strengthening. The sum of dislocation and precipitation strengthenings is less than the actual YS values in  Fig. 6 . The remaining YS increments, which is the difference between the actual YS values and the sum of dislocation and precipitation strengthening, should be attributed to other reasons. It is well known that the grain refinement could also contribute to work hardening due to the Hall–Petch effect. The coarse ferrite could recrystallize to refine ferrite grains during cold rolling, and some of them could be reversely transformed into ultrafine austenite grains during intercritical annealing ( Figs. 2b and 4 ). The coarse austenite grains transform into martensite during the yielding stage due to poor stability [ 19 ]; however, the ultrafine austenite grains could transform into martensite or twin during the later tensile deformation [ 8 , 11 ]. Therefore, the refinement of coarse austenite is not the main reason for the YS increment; such a result has been reported in Hu et al. [ 9 ]. However, both the ultrafine austenite and ferrite grains can contribute to the YS through the Hall–Petch mechanism.

sections.heading: Microstructure evolution during tensile deformation
paragraphs: Dislocations propagate and form the dense dislocation forests in the fine austenite grains during the initial deformation stage. However, the coarse austenite with poor stability transforms into martensite. Excessive stress concentration results in the nucleation of the previous twins. After further deformation, the secondary twins are generated and intersect with the previous twins, which can not only refine the microstructure but also effectively retard the movement of dislocations and gather dislocations at the grain boundaries [ 27 ], thus continuously increasing both the flow stress and strain hardening.

Fig. 10 
                          shows the microstructure evolution and the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns of sample I650 under different deformation stages. Martensite, which is transformed from coarse austenite, can be observed after 5% tensile strain ( Fig. 10 a–c), implying the coarse austenite transforms into martensite during the initial tensile deformation due to its poor stability [ 28 ]. The SAED pattern in  Fig. 10 b shows the typical [110] γ  and [111] ά , which indicates the [110] γ  and [111] ά  have the same orientation (the inset in  Fig. 10 b). Meanwhile, some of the newly formed nano twins could completely penetrate and subdivide the fine austenite grain ( Fig. 10 e), resulting in the formation of nanoscale austenite grains. The dense dislocation tangles are observed along and within the twin boundaries ( Fig. 10 e), leading to the interactions between dislocations and twins.

Owing to further deformation at 18% strain, after fracture, the primary twins and secondary twins intersect with each other at an angle of 70° ( Fig. 10 g), suggesting the presence of the interaction between twins. If so, the Hall–Petch effect will be extremely vital, and then more grain boundaries restrain the dislocation movement. The enlarged image of the marked area in  Fig. 10 g depicts the nano lamellar twins are full of high-density dislocations ( Fig. 10 h). In contrast, the dislocation density is higher than that in  Fig. 10 e, while the width of lamellar twin is smaller than that in  Fig. 10 e. The corresponding SAED pattern of deformation twins is shown in  Fig. 10 i. The persistent interactions between dislocations and twins significantly enhance the effective activation energy for dislocation movements, resulting in a dense distribution of dislocation tangles ( Fig. 10 h).

The effective stress, which acts on the chaotic mobile dislocations, is inversely proportional to the mobile dislocation density under a certain plastic strain rate [ 31 ]. Generally, the larger the number of mobile dislocations that cannot be moved during the initial deformation stage, the easier the effective stress acting on the mobile dislocations. Thus, the work hardening can be further launched [ 32 ].  Fig. 11 
                          shows the micro-models of deformation behaviors in the studied medium-Mn steel. The twin boundaries, as specific low-energy high-angle boundaries, are closely related to {111} planes of the austenite phase and effectively restrain dislocation motion [ 33 ], as shown in  Fig. 11 a. Some defects, such as a Shockley incomplete dislocation, may generate along twin boundaries as dislocations penetrating twin boundaries ( Fig. 11 b). Therefore, the twin boundaries can effectively assimilate mobile dislocations [ 31 ]. Due to various slip systems in austenite (FCC phase), the dislocations located within the deformation twins have a more abundant “soft” orientation to mobile compared with the BCC phase. At the initial deformation stage, the mobile dislocations may either be assimilated by twin boundaries or change to immovable dislocations due to the interactions between dislocation–dislocation and dislocation–twin boundaries, as shown in  Fig. 10 d. This result must lead to the decrease of mobile dislocations and the increase of effective stress acting on the mobile dislocations, ensuring the continuous work hardening behavior of medium-Mn steels.

sections.heading: The work hardening behavior
paragraphs:
Fig. 12 
                          shows that the true strain-work hardening rate curve varied with the austenite volume fraction of sample I650. It can be divided into four different stages, which are different from the previous reports [ 8 , 9 , 12 , 34 ]. The stage-1 corresponds to dislocation slip caused by ferrite deformation, meanwhile, the martensitic transformation of coarse austenite grains also can contribute to work hardening [ 9 ]. The stage-2 is related to the yield plateau, and the corresponding yield point elongation is in the range of 1.6%–8% ( Fig. 12 ). Martensitic transformation can result in an instantaneous increase of work hardening. However, the slight fluctuation of stage-2 implies it contributes a little in this stage. Moreover, 32% of austenite have been transformed during the first two stages. Therefore, the main reasons for Lüders plateau development are attributed to partial martensitic transformation and continuous interactions between dislocation and twin ( Fig. 10 d). The detailed discussion about Lüders plateau is analyzed in Section  4.4 .

In association with further deformation to stage-3, the ultrafine austenite grains with high stability can be transformed into martensite or twins. TRIP effect and TWIP effect occur during the large deformation, resulting in a better ductility. Here, the austenite volume fraction varies barely, implying the TRIP effect occurs only within a few austenite grains with high stability ( Fig. 10 d and g). The austenite grains with lamellar and equiaxed morphologies ( Fig. 2 b) in sample I650 can significantly enhance the work hardening [ 1 , 8–10 ], because the excessive stress concentration caused by plastic deformation promotes the aperiodic transformation of austenite to martensite or twin ( Fig. 10 ), which makes the strain–stress curve appear serrated ( Fig. 6 ).

The stage-4 corresponds to the PLC phenomenon, which shows the aperiodic fluctuation. Such a result may be related to the interaction between both dislocation–twin and twin–twin ( Fig. 10 g). Mobile dislocations accumulate within and along the lamellar twins ( Fig. 10 h), and the interactions between dislocation–twin and twin–twin contribute to the discontinuous yielding. However, the amplitude of fluctuation is much lower than that resulting from martensitic transformation [ 9 , 34 ].

                         F ) of samples before tensile deformation;  B  is the exponential factor and is considered the only determining parameter of austenite stability. Moreover, the higher the  B  value, the poorer the austenite stability. Based on the volume fractions of austenite in  Fig. 5 b and the exponential fitting, the  B  values of samples I650, I700, and I800 are calculated to be 6.37 ± 0.98, 7.85 ± 1.36, and 12.5 ± 1.24, respectively, as shown in  Fig. 13 
                         , which indicates that the austenite stability of sample I750 is the poorest. The austenite with lamellar and equiaxed morphologies ( Fig. 2 ) should be responsible for this result. It can provide a sustainable TRIP or TWIP effect at high strain due to a larger austenite fraction with proper stability. Therefore, samples I650 and I700 with lamellar and equiaxed austenite display the larger Lüders plateau than samples I750 with single equiaxed austenite.

However, the above discussion only considers the extensive austenite stability. The volume fraction [ 36 , 37 ] and grain size [ 38 ] of austenite significantly affect the propagation of Lüders plateau. It is well known that the coarse austenite with poor mechanical stability preferentially transforms into martensite at low strain and strongly affects the Lüders plateau propagation. Wang et al. [ 39 ] gave a conclusion that the strain-induced martensitic transformation should be responsible for the Lüders plateau propagation. Hu et al. [ 9 ] reported that the transformation ratio of austenite with poor mechanical stability might be the reliable reason for the Lüders plateau propagation, rather than the total volume fraction of transformed austenite. Unfortunately, they just provided a hypothesis and did not give a direct internal connection between them.

Since the coarse austenite fraction cannot be accurately acquired using XRD results ( Fig. 5 a) or EBSD results ( Fig. 4 ), it is replaced by the number fraction of coarse austenite using EBSD images ( Fig. 4 ). Here, the number fractions of coarse austenite are defined as the ratio between the number of coarse austenite grains and the number of total grains. Considering the average grain size of all samples are less than 0.6 μm, the austenite grain size larger than 1 μm is defined as coarse austenite grains. Surprisingly, the number fraction of coarse austenite grains decreases gradually with the increasing annealing temperature, the corresponding values of samples I650, I700, and I750 are 26.7%, 19.5%, and 10.6%, respectively. Such a result may be ascribed to the followed reasons. On the one hand, the ferrite grains recrystallize to refine grains at high annealing temperatures ( Fig. 4 ), leading to an increased total grain number. On the other hand, the coarse austenite grains suffer martensitic transformation during cooling, due to their poor chemical stability at higher annealing temperatures, resulting in the reduced number fractions of coarse austenite grains in samples I700 and I750.

Fig. 14 
                          shows a close relationship between coarse austenite number fraction and Lüders strain. It is obvious that the Lüders strain decreases with the decrease of coarse austenite number fraction. Thus, the number fraction of coarse austenite should be responsible for the Lüders plateau propagation, and there is a positive correlation between them. Such an exact mathematical relationship requires more studies in the future.

sections.heading: Analysis of Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect
paragraphs: The formation and propagation of PLC bands are considered a behavior of strain localization. So far, numerous literatures reported that both the nucleation and propagation of PLC bands should be attributed to the abundant TRIP effect in medium-Mn steels [ 40–42 ]. Yang et al. [ 40 ] reported that a volume fraction of the dynamically strain-induced martensite is the main reason for affecting the PLC behavior because the amount of strain-induced martensite increased with the increasing deformation level. The newly formed martensite, which had higher hardness than the matrix phases (ferrite and austenite), could effectively inhibit the PLC bands propagation. Such similar results have been verified in Refs. [ 43 , 44 ].

In present work, samples I650, I700 and I750 showed noticeable PLC bands during tensile deformation ( Fig. 5 a). In contrast, the PLC band in sample I750 is more regular ( Fig. 5 a). Such a result is attributed to the differences in austenite stability of samples. As shown in  Fig. 13 , the austenite stability continuously decreases with the increasing annealing temperature. In other words, more austenite grains in sample I750 have been transformed into martensite during the initial tensile deformation due to the poorest stability. A large amount of newly formed martensite (hard phase) acts as a barrier for the PLC band propagation. The remaining austenite grains with high stability cannot provide an explosive TRIP effect during the later tensile deformation. Under such large loading, high stress continues to propagate via PLC bands. For ensuring the PLC bands propagation under relatively low stress, a new region is needed to become a source for the PLC bands propagation. Therefore, the presence of both the non-transformed austenite with high stability and uniformly distributed barriers (strain-induced martensite) results in a more regular PLC band. In addition, the nano twin boundaries in sample I650 can effectively restrain the dislocation slip ( Fig. 10 g and h), resulting in the dynamic Hall–Petch mechanism and the dislocation pinning effect at twin boundaries [ 45 , 46 ]. Such a result can further accelerate the PLC band propagation.

In summary, the austenite with lamellar and equiaxed morphologies is manufactured at a proper annealing temperature. The recrystallization of ferrite during annealing and the martensitic transformation of coarse austenite with poor stability during cooling results in a reduced number fraction of relatively coarse austenite grains at higher annealing temperatures. As a result, the above two reasons lead to a wide TRIP-relate strain due to the different degrees of austenite mechanical stability. Such a result can be employed to tailor the microstructure of medium-Mn steel, and further demonstrate that the proper annealing temperature is necessary to obtain excellent mechanical properties of medium-Mn steel.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs:
Vanadium containing Mn steel manufactured by cold rolling and intercritically annealed at 650 °C display outstanding mechanical properties. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            The UTS (1450 MPa), YS (1210 MPa), and TE (18%) contribute to the best combination of mechanical properties in sample I650. The simultaneous involvement of V-carbide strengthening, dislocation strengthening, TRIP effect, and TWIP effect contributes to the outstanding mechanical properties. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Partial martensitic transformation and the complex interaction between dislocation and twin are responsible for the propagation of Lüders plateau front. And the interactions between dislocation–twin and twin–twin contribute to the subsequent aperiodic fluctuation of the work hardening curve, resulting in outstanding mechanical properties, especially the large ductility. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            Sample with lamellar and equiaxed austenite grains displays a larger Lüders plateau than a sample with single equiaxed/lamellar austenite grains. The number fraction of coarse austenite grains should be responsible for the propagation of Lüders plateau.
